commit.message:
Never trust a client-supplied role

signup accepts a role field so the client can be explicit, then ignores it.
Roles live in app_metadata, which only a service-role key can write; whatever
arrives, the account is created as a patient. user_metadata holds display and
contact details only and can grant nothing.

Middleware redirects a visitor with no credential to the correct sign-in door.
It checks presence only, never roles - a role check there would be a second,
weaker source of truth that could drift from the database.

The page guards exist for routing, not security: every route handler rechecks
the session and RLS enforces the rest. requireStaffPage has three outcomes,
not two, because someone who has registered deserves to be told their request
is pending rather than bounced to a login page they already passed.

FLOWCARE_DEMO_HOSPITAL_ID binds the demo staff accounts to a hospital that
exists in whichever database this deployment reads, so a staff dashboard full
of zeroes is a real empty day rather than a configuration gap.

Also assembles the Gemini-shaped test fixture at runtime: the value is
made-up, but a literal AIza... string trips secret scanners on push and would
bury a real finding in false positives.

commit.message:
Migrate authentication from NextAuth to Clerk-first architecture

Removes NextAuth as primary auth provider and establishes Clerk as the unified authentication system across the application. Retains internal Prisma database for role-based authorization, permissions, and business logic while delegating identity management (signup, login, MFA, password recovery) to Clerk.

Key changes:

- Replaces NextAuth configuration and session providers with Clerk SDK integration
- Updates auth utilities to fetch Clerk user data first, then sync to internal database for roles/permissions
- Removes custom login, register, and password reset pages in favor of Clerk-hosted flows
- Implements Clerk user synchronization service for bi-directional data consistency
- Adds payment verification audit logging and manual payment review workflow with recheck logic
- Migrates all API routes and server components to use Clerk's currentUser() and unified auth() helper
- Updates middleware to rely solely on Clerk authentication at the edge
- Removes legacy NextAuth routes, providers, and session configuration
- Adds support for claimed amount submission in manual UPI payment verification flow
- Integrates Clerk UI components (UserProfile, UserButton, SignOutButton) throughout the application
- Adds internal user context hook for accessing synced database user data in client components

The migration maintains backward compatibility for role-based access control while simplifying auth infrastructure and improving security posture.

fix(auth): close /refresh user-disable bypass; recheck users.enabled per request

A security review of the 0.8.x changes identified a HIGH-severity authz
gap introduced by the new POST /v1/auth/refresh endpoint:

The AppRole branch of /refresh deliberately re-checks app_roles for
existence, suspension, IP allowlist, and current policy list on every
refresh, so a suspended role can't keep extending its session. The
user-token branch (entered when payload.role_id is absent) did no
equivalent check - it copied payload.sub and payload.policies straight
into a new SignJWT call. Combined with the global authMiddleware doing
no per-request users-table lookup (no enabled check, no JWT denylist,
no min_iat), and the fact that all UI users are minted with
policies:["admin"], a disabled or deleted user holding a still-valid
JWT could perpetually self-renew that token via /refresh and retain
full admin indefinitely.

Two-layer fix:

1. /v1/auth/refresh user branch (src/api/auth.ts):
   - Strip "user:" prefix from payload.sub, look up the users row.
   - Reject 401 if the row is missing or enabled = 0.
   - Re-derive the policy claim from server state rather than echoing
     payload.policies.

2. authMiddleware (src/auth/middleware.ts):
   - Accept an optional Database argument. When provided, recheck
     users.enabled on every request for JWTs whose sub starts with
     "user:". Disable/delete now takes effect at the very next request,
     not at the residual JWT TTL window. AppRole JWTs are unaffected
     (AppRole revocation flows through role deletion + /v1/rotate).
   - src/index.ts wires the existing db reference through.

Tests: 356 pass. New coverage for refresh refusing disabled and deleted
users, middleware rejecting same on protected routes, and refresh
re-deriving policies from server state.

Bump to 0.8.2.

commit.message:
Recheck account status on the Socket.IO handshake

The handshake middleware only called verifyAccessToken, so a valid signature
was the whole check. Unlike the HTTP path (ProtectionService), it never
reloaded the user, which meant:

- Deactivating an account left that user's socket connected and still
  receiving their notifications until the token happened to expire.
- A student whose approval was revoked kept their live connection.
- A deleted user's socket stayed open.
- The role came from the token claim, so a role change did not take effect
  for the lifetime of the socket.

Socket.IO also authenticates once, at the handshake, and never again. The
connection therefore outlived its access token indefinitely: a socket opened
once stayed authorised for as long as it stayed connected.

- Reload the user in the handshake and reject unless isActive and approved.
- Take socket.userRole from the database, not the token claim.
- Disconnect the socket when its access token expires; the client reconnects
  with a refreshed one.
- Extract the middleware as authenticateSocket so it is testable without
  pulling in socket.io-client.
- Export isAccountApproved from AuthServices so the handshake applies exactly
  the same approval rule as the HTTP path rather than a copy of it.

Also drop the "or cookie" comment on the token lookup — there is no cookie
fallback in the code; the browser client sends handshake.auth.token.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Task #35: Re-validate account state on every authenticated request

Vulnerability: bearer tokens (7-day JWTs) kept granting access after the
underlying account was soft-deleted, because authMiddleware only verified
the JWT signature/expiry and trusted embedded userId/role claims without
ever consulting the database.

Fix in artifacts/api-server/src/lib/auth.ts:
- Added loadActiveUser(userId) helper that fetches id, role, deletedAt
  from the users table and returns null when the row is missing or
  soft-deleted (deletedAt set).
- Converted authMiddleware to async: verifies JWT, then runs
  loadActiveUser and 401s ("Account is no longer active") if the row is
  gone/soft-deleted. Sets req.userRole from the live DB role rather than
  the token claim, so role demotions take effect immediately and
  adminOnly / traderOnly / customerOnly automatically respect the new
  role.
- Converted optionalAuth to async: same DB recheck — invalid token or
  deleted account simply yields anonymous (no userId set), then next().
- Wrapped the DB lookup in try/catch so a database error returns 500
  instead of silently authenticating.

Also fixed artifacts/api-server/src/routes/auth.ts /api/auth/me to return
401 when the loaded user has deletedAt (was previously returning the
soft-deleted record as if active).

Deviation from initial draft: did NOT block users.isActive=false. That
flag tracks subscription state for traders (false during onboarding
before payment, false after cancellation) and login intentionally allows
those users in — see /auth/login. Blocking it in middleware would have
locked traders out of onboarding endpoints. Documented this rule on
loadActiveUser so future maintainers preserve the alignment.

Verification: api-server typecheck passes; reviews.test.ts (14/14) passes
against the new async middleware. Architect review: PASS.

[T-12] Move admin authorization to Clerk publicMetadata, gate it in middleware (#246)

* [T-12] Move admin authorization to Clerk publicMetadata, gate it in middleware

api/sellers/admin/route.js resolved admin status with its own
module-level Map + setInterval cache of Mongo's User.role, keyed by
Clerk userId - a per-instance cache in serverless, with an interval that
never gets cleared. The /admin/sellers page itself only checked for a
session, no role at all; the API behind it was the only real gate.

- src/middleware.js now gates /admin(.*) and /api/(.*)/admin(.*) before
  any handler runs: no session -> sign-in redirect (pages) / 401 (API);
  session but publicMetadata.role !== 'admin' -> redirect home (pages) /
  403 (API). The decision table itself lives in a pure function
  (src/utils/lib/adminAccess.ts) so it's unit-testable without mocking
  Clerk's request-signing internals.
- api/sellers/admin/route.js dropped the Map, the setInterval, and its
  own currentUser()-based check - it now trusts the middleware, the same
  way isProtectedRoute already gates seller-only pages with no per-page
  recheck.
- Went with clerkClient().users.getUser(userId) over reading
  publicMetadata from sessionClaims: the latter needs the session token
  customized in Clerk's dashboard, an infrastructure change this repo
  avoids after the T-64 incident. Same Backend API cost class the old
  currentUser() call already paid, just only for admin-route hits now.
- Caught by re-checking the build output: removing the route's req param
  left it with nothing request-specific, so Next optimized it as static
  - it would have served one Mongo snapshot from build time forever.
  Fixed with export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'.
- scripts/set-admin-metadata.mjs migrates existing Mongo admins into
  Clerk publicMetadata, reusing backfill-clerk-id.mjs's instance guard.
  Dry run against the real database found 4 admins (3 ready, 1 with no
  clerkId) - not applied yet, left for a deliberate decision since it
  writes to real accounts on the shared Clerk instance.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* [T-12] Record why the admin metadata migration can't apply yet

Tried npm run set-admin-metadata --apply --permitir-desarrollo against
the real database. comprobarInstancia()'s cross-instance check refused,
and checking all 3 target admins individually confirmed why: all three
clerkIds 404 against the Clerk instance that actually serves the live
site. They're stale, left over from the old production instance -
T-64b's reclaim flow was never run for any of the three (confirmed for
the project owner's own account: a single User document, still holding
the pre-T-64 clerkId).

This is a real, pre-existing prerequisite (T-64b), not a bug in the
migration script or something T-12 introduced. Documented in both T-12
(what blocks it) and T-64b (a concrete number: at least 3 of the 63
unreclaimed accounts identified).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
fix(triage): close authority surface gaps for viewer roles, grants, and legacy link

Read-only viewer principals are now denied before every lifecycle write, both at the transport and re-read from the users table inside the transaction, in teamed and un-teamed habitats alike. The remote action scope vocabulary becomes a single shared catalog that the type union, contributor middleware, and the admin grant-provisioning schema all derive from, so triage.route grants can finally be created through the real admin API instead of only direct repository writes. The undocumented legacy unlink shape is removed: unlinking now fails fast with a stable code and deprecation telemetry, with no database reads, and the retained first-link shape requires human habitat-write authority and applies link and route fingerprint as one writer-reserved single-column update, closing the two-write crash window. Lifecycle actor authority becomes required with a grep-able test-only sentinel, so a transport can no longer silently skip the in-transaction recheck, and the API and troubleshooting docs record the removed shape, the client-upgrade remediation, and the new viewer denial.

commit.message:
Task #35: Re-validate account state on every authenticated request

Vulnerability: bearer tokens (7-day JWTs) kept granting access after the
underlying account was soft-deleted (`deletedAt`) or disabled
(`isActive=false`), because `authMiddleware` only verified the JWT
signature/expiry and trusted the embedded `userId`/`role` claims.

Fix in artifacts/api-server/src/lib/auth.ts:
- Added `loadActiveUser(userId)` helper that fetches `id`, `role`,
  `isActive`, `deletedAt` from the users table and returns null when the
  account is missing, soft-deleted, or inactive.
- Converted `authMiddleware` to async: verifies JWT, then runs
  `loadActiveUser` and 401s ("Account is no longer active") if the row is
  gone/disabled. Sets `req.userRole` from the live DB role rather than the
  token claim, so role demotions take effect immediately and adminOnly /
  traderOnly / customerOnly automatically respect the new role.
- Converted `optionalAuth` to async: same DB recheck — invalid token or
  inactive/deleted account simply yields anonymous (no userId set), then
  next().
- Added try/catch around the DB lookup so a database error returns 500
  instead of silently authenticating.

Also fixed artifacts/api-server/src/routes/auth.ts `GET /api/auth/me` to
return 401 when the loaded user has `deletedAt` or `!isActive` (was
previously returning the deleted/disabled record as if active).

Verification: api-server typecheck passes; existing reviews.test.ts suite
(14/14) passes against the new async middleware. Architect review: PASS.

perf(admin): cut round trips on every panel page (#1154)

* feat(api): let an app hand over its own Supabase client

setSupabaseClient registers a client the app already owns as the shared one, so services and the app's auth use one session. The admin panel needs it: it signs in with @supabase/ssr (cookies) and used to copy that session into this package's localStorage client with setSession on every page, a network call each time. The handed-over client keeps its own locks and gets the same realtime auth pump. The timeout fetch moves to its own side-effect-free module so the admin can give it to that client.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EbnC6H75XT6LqrciPs9Gzi

* perf(admin): one Supabase client, one user read, role from the middleware

The panel now gives its @supabase/ssr client to @tricigo/api, so nothing copies sessions. useAdminUser is a context read once with getSession (no network) instead of getUser plus setSession in each of ~15 components. The middleware verifies the token locally with getClaims, keeps role lookups for a minute and shares them between requests that arrive together (the menu prefetch fired 39 in 10 s, each with two Supabase calls), checks is_active, and writes the role to a cookie the role provider reads instead of querying users.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EbnC6H75XT6LqrciPs9Gzi

* perf(admin): stop duplicate requests on every page

One SOS subscription for the whole panel instead of one per component, one dashboard-metrics request shared by the bell and the dashboard, and the pending-promotions count every 2 minutes instead of on every navigation.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EbnC6H75XT6LqrciPs9Gzi

* perf(admin): driver detail in fewer round trips

The work wallet comes embedded in the profile request (naming wallet_accounts_user_id_fkey: the table has two keys to users) instead of a second request after it, and the documents are signed in one createSignedUrls call instead of one per document.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EbnC6H75XT6LqrciPs9Gzi

* perf(admin): load only the panel's Spanish texts

initAdminI18n loads the admin namespace in Spanish (119 KB) instead of every namespace in three languages (787 KB). @tricigo/i18n is marked side-effect free so useTranslation no longer drags config.ts in. First-load JS of most admin pages drops from 525-568 kB to 310-354 kB.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EbnC6H75XT6LqrciPs9Gzi

* docs: admin panel speed rules

What made the panel slow (chained round trips, not the database), the rules that keep it fast, how to measure it, and the pending database part.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EbnC6H75XT6LqrciPs9Gzi

* fix(admin): middleware treats any getClaims failure as signed out and rechecks the session

getClaims rethrows errors that are not AuthErrors (a JWT whose exp passed while the cookie looked fresh, an unknown alg), which made a 500 page: now they send the person to login. The account lookup, cached per session and minute, also asks GoTrue whether the session still exists (getUser), so signing out everywhere or a block closes the pages within a minute, as when getUser ran on every request. A session GoTrue no longer has goes to login, not to the unauthorized notice.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EbnC6H75XT6LqrciPs9Gzi

* fix(admin): SOS list reloads after a dropped connection

The shared SOS store read the list once per session, and realtime does not replay the events of a gap: an SOS created while an admin's link was down never showed until a full reload. It now loads right away, again every time the channel joins or rejoins, and retries a failed load after 30 s. Rows that arrive during a load are applied on top of its result. Each start uses its own channel topic, so a channel still closing cannot swallow the new subscription.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EbnC6H75XT6LqrciPs9Gzi

* perf(admin): fewer requests left over

useIsSuperAdmin reads the role the panel already has instead of calling is_super_admin on every mount of seven pages; the bell asks fresh metrics when it is opened; the driver detail embed filters the work wallet in the request.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EbnC6H75XT6LqrciPs9Gzi

The middleware's per-session GoTrue check and the SOS reload on reconnection.

feat(auth): Task 1.1 — Auth.js v5 infrastructure & session hardening (#1)

* feat(auth): Task 1.1 — Auth.js v5 infrastructure & session hardening

- Install next-auth@beta, @auth/prisma-adapter, bcryptjs + TS types
- Install @typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin + parser; update .eslintrc.json
- PasswordHash value object: bcrypt cost 12, 12-char min enforcement
- Auth.js config: Credentials provider, database sessions, 30-day rolling
  expiry, httpOnly+SameSite=Strict cookie, deactivated-user sign-in block
- Prisma singleton in lib/shared/prisma.ts
- Next.js route handler at app/api/auth/[...nextauth]/route.ts
- Middleware: redirect unauthenticated users to /login
- Extend Auth.js types to include role on Session + User
- Vitest config: add @/* path alias resolution
- AUT-auth.test.ts: implement AC-1 (12-char min) and AC-2 (httpOnly session)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(auth): address MMR findings F-003 F-004 F-005 F-006

F-003: remove POWER_USER default in session callback — deny session if role
  is missing rather than silently granting elevated privileges
F-004: remove redundant signIn callback status check — authorize() already
  verifies user.status === 'ACTIVE' before returning credentials
F-005: validate callbackUrl is a same-origin path before embedding it in
  the redirect URL, preventing open-redirect attacks
F-006: replace `req.auth: unknown` cast with `Session | null` for type safety;
  add `export const runtime = 'nodejs'` to support Prisma-backed session
  revocation checks (deferred to Task 1.4 per scope)

with Credentials provider in next-auth@5.0.0-beta.31

P0 fix: Next.js middleware requires Edge runtime — cannot use Node.js runtime
P1 fix: Auth.js v5 Credentials provider requires JWT strategy (not database)

Architecture restructure:
- lib/auth/auth.config.ts: edge-safe config — no Prisma, JWT strategy, pages,
  jwt/session callbacks that embed id+role into the signed token
- lib/auth/index.ts: Node.js-only — merges authConfig + Credentials provider
  (with Prisma user lookup) + PrismaAdapter
- middleware.ts: edge-safe — imports authConfig directly, not the full index.ts;
  JWT signature verification requires no DB per request
- lib/auth/types.d.ts: extend JWT type to include id and role fields
- AUT-auth.test.ts AC-2: update assertion to expect 'jwt' strategy

revocation store (Upstash/KV) per the comment in middleware.ts.

commit.message:
Harden authentication and lock down the deployment

Closes an anonymous privilege escalation, moves the session out of
localStorage, and adds the surrounding hardening for a single-owner
deployment with a public guest demo.

Authentication
- register no longer reads `role` from the request body; it is hardcoded to
  GUEST. Previously any anonymous caller could mint a SOVEREIGN token, which
  authenticate() trusted without rechecking, granting full read/write on the
  live archive and both admin routes.
- Registration is disabled unless ALLOW_REGISTRATION=true. There is no
  registration UI, and these accounts' tenant databases did not match the
  reaper's naming so they were never reclaimed.
- The JWT is issued as an httpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure cookie rather
  than stored in localStorage, so page scripts cannot read it. SameSite
  Strict is what now defends state-changing routes against CSRF.
- SOVEREIGN is re-read from the database on each request instead of being
  trusted from the token. Guests keep the zero-lookup path.
- Changing the password stamps passwordChangedAt, retiring sessions issued
  earlier on every other device.
- Session lifetimes: sovereign 30d -> 7d; guest 2h, matching the sandbox TTL
  so a token cannot outlive the database it points at.
- Failed logins limited to 10 per 15 minutes per IP; successes do not count.

Guest demo
- Per-IP rate limit plus a concurrent-sandbox cap that reaps expired
  sandboxes before it would refuse anyone, and fails open if the cluster
  will not report database counts.
- Removed the beforeunload logout beacon. sendBeacon cannot set an
  Authorization header so it never did anything; once the session moved to a
  cookie it started working, and beforeunload fires on an ordinary refresh,
  silently destroying a visitor's sandbox mid-demo.

Hardening
- Strict CSP, HSTS, frame-ancestors none, nosniff, no-referrer and a
  Permissions-Policy. The document and API policies are separate, defined
  once in backend/utils/securityHeaders.js and mirrored in vercel.json.
- Image proxy re-validates every redirect hop against the SSRF guard, serves
  only bitmap content types, caps bodies at 8MB, and refuses third-party
  hotlinking. Previously it would echo attacker-controlled text/html back on
  the app's own origin.
- Third-party synopsis HTML is sanitized through a tag allowlist before
  rendering.
- trust proxy set, so rate limiting buckets per client rather than sharing
  one bucket behind Vercel's proxy.
- CORS declines unknown origins instead of throwing, which previously
  produced a 500 that bypassed the header middleware.
- Added a terminal error handler; six handlers no longer return raw driver
  messages.

Maintenance
- Sandbox reaper moved off a module-scope setInterval, which never fired on
  serverless, onto a secret-gated endpoint driven hourly by the workflow.
- Removed six unused dependencies including puppeteer and playwright, and
  regenerated package-lock.json so they are no longer installed for the
  lambda.
- ESLint config moved to the repo root; the previous script linted a single
  file and the whole src tree was never checked.

Track B ran in parallel with Track A from the first hour, three agents, never
more, per HANDOFF 02 section 26. Each was read-only on the codebase and wrote
exactly one file. None of them ran git. The lead committed everything.

  AGENT2_ENGINEERING_BACKEND_DB_SECURITY   3,665 lines   157 recommendations
  AGENT3_FRONTEND_DESIGN_MOTION_QA         2,942 lines   172 recommendations

section 8 requires: evidence, action, reason, impact, effort, risk, priority.
Critical 30, High 166, Medium 228, Nice-to-have 54, Future 3.

Each report states near the top, rather than at the end, what its agent did not
check and did not do. Those sections are the most useful part of each file and
they are long: no agent reached the live database, Agent 1 rendered nothing,
Agent 3 never saw a signed-in screen, and none of the 82 Playwright specs was

commit.message:
Every route declares what it needs, and the socket knows who is on it

Phase 3: enforcement. The CMS is closed.

`withActor` runs once, straight after the bindings, and resolves an identity —
it refuses nothing. What each route *requires* is declared at that route's own
mount (`requireAccess<Env>(rt, MANAGE)`), so the gate is visible beside the
handler rather than in a table of path patterns somewhere else. One middleware
covers both currencies, a minimum role for a person and a scope for a token,
because they are the same requirement said twice and splitting them is how the
two drift apart.

The memoised-thunk discipline survives intact: `resolveActor` reads no D1 for
a request that presents neither a cookie nor a bearer token, so `/schema`, a
404 and a refused socket upgrade still cost the database nothing.
`auth: 'open'` short-circuits on the *mode*, never on the actor — `allows(null,
…)` is unconditionally false, so the predicate can never be the reason an
unauthenticated request got through.

Two gates that are not obvious from the spec's route table. `?_folio=preview`
lives outside `basePath`, so the app's middleware never sees it, and it renders
a *draft*: without a check of its own, appending that flag to any URL read
unpublished content on a site that had otherwise closed its editor completely.
It now refuses by handing the request *back* to the host rather than by
answering 401, so to a visitor the flag simply means nothing and they get the
ordinary published page. And `/users` / `/tokens` 404 under `auth: 'open'`
rather than standing open: there is no admin there and no way to become one.

**The subtle trap, handled.** `broadcast`'s pre-hello quarantine was "has an
attachment", which worked only because `hello` was what created one. Attaching
a verified identity at upgrade time gives every socket an attachment
immediately, so that test would have admitted every lurker — a delta delivered
to a socket with no watermark, which is a silent gap in the sync engine dressed
up as a login change. The membership test is now an explicit `joined` flag, set
by `hello`, and `peers()` and the departure broadcast use it too. Three tests
pin it, including one where the lurker holds a perfectly good session.

`presenceOf` is also new and is not cosmetic: presence used to be a spread of
the attachment, and the attachment now holds `role`, `session` and `expiresAt`.
Spreading it would have broadcast a session id to every other editor.

Identity now arrives as a header on the upgrade, which is trustworthy for one
reason: a Durable Object namespace is not publicly addressable, so the only way
to reach the object is through the Worker that set it. `withIdentity` therefore
*always* sets or deletes the header and never leaves it alone — this route
forwards the client's own request, and a conditional set would let a client
assert an identity by sending the header itself. `hello`'s `actor`/`name`/
`colour` become advisory: they keep their place in the frame, so no protocol
bump and no broken old tab, they simply stop being believed. Under
`auth: 'open'` they are still the only identity there is, and are still taken.

Revocation costs one D1 read a minute per socket, not one per keystroke
(checkpoint 5). The expiry rides in the attachment and is free; the D1 re-check
is bounded by `SESSION_RECHECK_MS`. A test asserts the *inverse* too — that a
deleted session does **not** close the socket inside the window — because
without it nothing stops that re-check from quietly becoming per-frame. A
transient D1 failure is deliberately not treated as a revocation: signing an
editor out mid-sentence because the database blinked is worse than the bounded
window this design already accepts.

One sanctioned behaviour change beyond the gates: `x-folio-actor` is no longer
read, and neither is `actor` in the checkpoint body. History records the
session's own `users.id`, `token:<name>` for a script, and **null** under
`auth: 'open'`, where there is genuinely nobody to attribute a change to. Four
hook tests in http.test.ts now assert that null, and the test that bounded the
old header's length now asserts the header is ignored entirely — bounding a
self-reported actor was only ever making a lie tidy. An old tab that still
sends it is not refused.

A role change revokes that user's sessions. The bounded window checkpoint 5
accepts for a revocation is not one worth accepting for a downgrade an admin
just made on purpose.

Origin checking rather than CSRF tokens (decision 4), narrowed twice on
purpose: only for cookie-authenticated mutations, since a cookie is the only
credential a browser attaches ambiently, and an absent `Origin` passes, since
that is curl or a script rather than a page that can borrow anyone's cookie.

30 tests added (1127 → 1157).

commit.message:
Implement password reset and OTP resend; map the remaining error codes

/auth/forgot-password, /auth/reset-password and /auth/resend-otp were one-line
stubs returning success unconditionally — no email sent, no password changed —
while emailService.js already held complete bilingual reset templates and
auth.js imported sendResetPasswordEmail without ever calling it. This was a
built feature left unwired, which is why it would pass a QA click-through.

My own earlier commit made it worse: those routes previously returned bare
English, and giving them codes turned the lie into a polished localized one in
two languages. A locked-out user was told a reset link was on its way.

Implementation reuses what already existed: resetPasswordToken and
resetPasswordExpires were already on the User model, and passwordResetAt was
already read by the login route to skip OTP for 24h but written by nothing.

- The reset token is stored as a SHA-256 hash and only the raw value is
  emailed, so a database leak yields no usable links. Single-use, 1-hour
  expiry matching what the email copy promises.
- New passwords are hashed with bcrypt explicitly — there is no pre-save hook
  on User, so assigning plaintext would have stored it in the clear. A test
  now fails if that hook ever appears, since the route would need rechecking.
- forgot-password and resend-otp return an identical response whether or not
  the account exists, and swallow email failures, so neither becomes an
  account-enumeration oracle. reset-password uses one code for "unknown token"
  and "expired" alike.
- Both email-sending routes now sit behind a dedicated limiter keyed on the
  target address, so one victim cannot be mail-bombed and burning that budget
  no longer blocks legitimate logins from the same IP.

Session revocation: a stateless 7-day JWT meant a password reset left an
attacker's existing token working for the rest of the week. User gains
tokensValidFrom; the reset sets it; the auth middleware rejects any token
whose iat predates it. This costs no extra query — getPrincipalState widens
the projection the disabled-check already reads behind its 30s cache, and the
route calls invalidatePrincipal so revocation is immediate. UserContext treats
the resulting SESSION_REVOKED as terminal, like ACCOUNT_DISABLED.

Also maps the 5 codes that reached the UI unmapped (ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED,
INSUFFICIENT_ROLE, ORG_CREATING, PLAN_CHECK_ERROR, USER_NOT_FOUND) plus 4 that
were handled by hand-rolled chains, so Hero and Profile now resolve through
the shared mapper. Every one of the 66 backend codes is now mapped.

Fixed while here: ResetPasswordPage validated a 6-character minimum against
the server's 8, and passwordMinLength still said "6" in both locales.

Verified: backend 81/81, frontend 33/33, production build clean at CI=true.
Not verified — that an email actually arrives; that needs a run against SES.

commit.message:
fix: organization scoping, permission checks and environment isolation (#371)

* fix(api): scope compose, manifest diff, database and DNS procedures to the caller's organization

Several org-scoped procedures took a project or resource id from their
input and looked it up by that id alone, without checking which
organization it belongs to. Each now scopes its own lookup to the caller's
organization, and an id outside it reads as not found:

- compose.* (get, list, updateContent, redeploy, delete,
  setDockerSocketGrant, and the stack variables) through
  getComposeRecordInOrg / listComposeRecordsInOrg;
- project.manifest.diff with an inline manifest;
- database.ephemeralList / ephemeralRevoke;
- the postgres setPlacement procedure;
- data.openSession for a managed database;
- service.domains.autoConfigureDns (the route lookup joins the project).

storage.presign for a PUT (upload) URL now also requires backup:create.

Ref: od-5sj7.145 od-5sj7.154 od-5sj7.167 od-5sj7.185 od-5sj7.186 od-5sj7.188

* fix(auth): close the organization plugin's team write endpoints over HTTP

Teams are modelled on the project table, so the plugin's team writes
(create, update, remove, member add/remove, set-active) would write project
rows directly, outside project.create and project.delete. Nothing in the
product calls them; they are now disabled like /api-key/create. Team reads
stay open.

Ref: od-5sj7.166

* fix(api): typed refusals instead of 500s; a cancelled update run stays settled

- project.stack.save answers 400 INVALID_STACK for a file that is not a
  stack and 409 CONFLICT for a stale version; project.stack.apply answers
  409 STACK_NOT_SAVED before any save.
- organization.setCloudflareConfig answers 400 when Cloudflare rejects the
  token or no zone is picked.
- sso.listProviders refuses an API key with a 403.
- data.testConnection answers 404 for an unknown connection.
- After system.cancelUpdate, the cancelled run's background steps no longer
  append to it or mark it succeeded.

Ref: od-5sj7.155 od-5sj7.168 od-5sj7.169

* fix(org): requests act in the organization they state; refused switches keep the session; creates are idempotent

- Org-scoped procedures refuse (409 ORGANIZATION_SWITCHED) a request whose
  stated organization (the x-otterdeploy-organization header, or an
  organizationId in the input) is not the session's active one, instead of
  acting in the session's organization. The dashboard states the page's
  organization on every call while the session is in it, so a tab left open
  after another tab switched organizations no longer writes into the other
  one. The header is allowed in CORS.
- /organization/set-active for an organization the user does not belong to
  is refused without clearing the session's active organization, and a
  session with no active organization answers a typed 409
  NO_ACTIVE_ORGANIZATION instead of a 500. The org-scoped middleware moves
  to authz/org-scope-middleware.ts.
- apiKeys.create and /organization/invite-member claim the request for 30
  seconds (new request_claim table), so a double submit or a retry after a
  lost response makes one key / one invitation; the repeat gets a 409. A
  failed create gives its claim back; an explicit invite resend is exempt.
- Member and invitation references with control characters are refused as
  invalid input.

Ref: od-5sj7.159 od-5sj7.172 od-5sj7.161

* fix(api): permission checks on state-changing git, deployment, database and backup procedures

These sat on the bare org-scoped builder, which only checks membership, so
a read-only API key or a role without the permission reached them:

- git provider writes (startConnect, startManifest, refreshRepos,
  refetchPermissions, connectPublicRepo) now need project:update;
- git.disconnect and git.deleteProvider are org-wide and need
  organization:update: owners and admins only, and no API key;
- deployment.cancel needs service:deploy, like restart and rollback;
- the postgres draftCredentials procedure needs database:create;
- backups.destinations.test needs backup:run.

Ref: od-5sj7.187

* fix(api): send secret-provider requests through the outbound egress policy

The Vault / Infisical / Doppler client used plain fetch. It now goes
through the same egress policy as webhooks and registries: loopback,
private, link-local and cloud-metadata addresses are refused unless the
operator put the address on the egress allowlist, DNS answers are checked
and pinned, every redirect hop is re-checked, and responses are size-capped.
Plain HTTP stays allowed for self-hosted providers on a LAN.

Ref: od-5sj7.189

* fix(env): each environment's hosts reach its own container; a private environment gates them

service_resource.service_name is the base name a production and a staging
service share; the deploy path runs a non-main environment as
`<base>-<env>`. Route writes (add, recheck, rename, expose, generate), the
service delete teardown and the status reads used the base name, so a
non-main environment's host was routed to the main environment's container
and its delete addressed the wrong one. They now resolve the runtime name
(routers/service/runtime-name.ts), and a non-main environment's generated
host carries the same suffix.

The forward_auth authorizer now applies the same rule as the edge: a route
is gated when its own switch is on or its environment is private.

Generate domain resolves the platform's host directly instead of through
the publicDomain mirror of the primary route, so it mints a host beside a
primary custom domain instead of returning that domain.

Ref: od-5sj7.207 od-5sj7.206

* fix(protection): deployment protection applies to every host of a service

The settings card has one protection switch, bound to whichever of the
service's routes it found first, and setProtection wrote only that row, so
with a custom domain and a generated host only one of them was gated.

Protection is now a property of the service: setProtection and
setAccessPin write every route of the resource (previews included); a host
added later is created protected with the same PIN; the edge and the
forward_auth authorizer treat any protected route as protecting all of the
resource's routes (caddy/service-protection.ts); a guest invited from one
host signs in on any of them, and removing one revokes it on all. No UI
change.

Ref: od-5sj7.213

commit.message:
feat(T-203): project services on ProjectScope (#266)

* feat(T-203): project services on ProjectScope

Every project service reads ProjectScope from context. Each project
endpoint declares what it needs with a RequiresProject annotation and
runs behind the ProjectAccess middleware, which resolves the scope and
checks the grants before the handler runs. MCP tools declare theirs next
to each tool through projectTool. Upload tokens and the attachment and
Figma thumbnail routes load their user, provide CurrentUser and resolve
the scope through Access themselves.

Checks that depend on the data stay in the service as pure policies in
@pp/access/policies. Tickets check each changed field: content needs
ticket:update (or update_own on your own ticket), status
ticket:transition, assignees ticket:assign. Comments need moderate, or
update_own/delete_own on your own comment. Sprints and milestones need
sprint:manage, other groups epic:manage. Callers without github:read get
tickets and project detail without GitHub data. ProjectDetail carries the
caller's permissions, and client is assignable.

Org owners and admins without a project role read all content, manage
members and archive or delete projects. Developers and PMs can connect
a GitHub repo. Access.projectsInOrg is the single source of project
visibility, and CurrentOrg is gone.

One RcMap-based KeyedLock replaces the hand-rolled lock maps in ticket
documents, groups and the library.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(T-203): close the gaps from the access review

- split authorizes the retained ticket against the source and new tickets
  against the create defaults, rechecked on the locked document
- split needs sprint:manage to move the original out of its sprint and
  github:write to detach its branch or PR
- hasBranch/hasPr filters need github:read in list, count and sections
- the active timer is only returned for a project in this org where the
  caller has time:read

The split and filter rules are TicketPolicy.canSplit and canQuery.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(T-203): split keeps the original's branch and PR

The retained ticket keeps its GitHub association and only the new tickets
start without one, so splitting no longer needs github:write and the
detach warning in the split dialog is gone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(T-203): finer sprint permissions and trusted clients

- sprint actions split into manage, add_ticket, remove_ticket and reorder;
  developers and clients add to and reorder sprints, only pms plan them or
  take tickets out, and moving a ticket out of another active sprint counts
  as taking it out
- clients edit any ticket and change status and assignees, but can't delete;
  ticket update_own is gone, so archiving is a plain ticket:update on the
  endpoint
- the sprint board's status change goes through Tickets with transition and
  status checks; Groups only reorders
- split pieces may copy the original's status and sprint; only newly added
  assignees must be project members
- ticket create and update reject unknown statuses; creating a sprint takes
  its tickets out of other active sprints
- the About doc needs docs:write, the org member directory member:read
- docs: matrix updated, admins may add themselves as pm

The rules that depend on the request live in @pp/access/policies:
GroupPolicy.can and canChangeTickets for sprint membership,
ProjectPolicy.canUpdate for the About doc versus settings, and the
reworked TicketPolicy.canChange and canSplit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* refactor(T-203): readable roleOnProject

The org-to-project grants are a table, and seeing the project, the
project role's grants and the org role's grants each get a name.
projectPermissions is renamed to roleOnProject.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(T-203): recheck access after an upload body and guard split's sprint write

- upload receive resolves the uploader's access again inside the
  transaction, after the body is buffered and before the S3 write
- setSprintMembership takes the sprint the caller expects the ticket to be
  in and fails with Conflict when it changed; split only writes the
  original's membership when it moves it, and only restores it then
- the comment persistence tests migrate their database instead of relying
  on another test file having done it

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(T-203): keep sprint moves and creates whole, and report the caller's new permissions

- moveInGroup persists the ticket status inside the group lock, just
  before the reorder write, so a failed status update leaves the
  saved order untouched.
- Creating a sprint undoes its evictions and removes itself when an
  eviction write fails.
- replayDetail derives ProjectDetail.permissions from the caller's
  current project role, so changing your own role returns the grants
  you now have.
- The ticket request benchmark fixture carries permissions, banner and
  iconImage again, so the script decodes it on start.
- KeyedLock's service shape is a Readonly type alias.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(T-203): leave a project through its own endpoint

POST /orgs/:orgSlug/projects/:slug/leave removes the caller's own
membership under the project lock, keeps the last-PM rule, unassigns
their active tickets, and returns no content, so the response never
carries a project the caller may no longer read. removeMember now
refuses to target the caller with Validation remove_self.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(T-203): finish leaving despite a broken ticket and name the sprint options type

- leave and removeMember no longer fail after the membership delete
  committed: ticket cleanup is best-effort, so their error types drop
  the ticket document errors.
- The sprint membership options are a SprintMembershipOptions Readonly
  type alias.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(T-203): name the Figma links harness input as a Readonly alias

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

---------

Co-authored-by: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

API hardening: RBAC hole, unauthenticated endpoint, false RESOLVED, audit trail (planning#162, #194) (#21)

API hardening batch: four independently-verified auth/API defects, in
the order **1 → 2 → 4 → 3** (what unblocks what, not severity).

## 1. RBAC hole — a VIEWER could change scan intensity

`PATCH /api/targets/{id}` was guarded by bare `get_current_user`.
`TargetPatch` carries `aggressiveness`, which governs how hard this
system probes a third party's infrastructure — so any authenticated
VIEWER could raise the outbound scan tier one target at a time, while
being correctly blocked from doing it in bulk. Now `require_role(ADMIN,
INTEGRATION_ADMIN)`, matching the four sibling routes on the same object
(`bulk_set_aggressiveness`, `bulk_recheck_targets`,
`bulk_delete_targets`, `delete_target`). This gated planning#193, which
puts an `is_ma` safety control on the same endpoint.

**On testing this — the approach, stated because "we tested it" and "we
tested the thing that was broken" are different claims here.**

There is no `TestClient` pattern anywhere in this suite. The convention
is calling router functions directly with `_=None` for the auth
dependency, which supplies the parameter by hand so **FastAPI never
resolves the `Depends(...)` at all** — `patch_target(..., _=None)`
returns 200 for a VIEWER both before and after this fix. A test written
to the local idiom would have passed against the bug.

The defect is a route *declaring the wrong dependency*, so the test has
to go through the layer that resolves dependencies. `test_api_rbac.py`
introduces `TestClient` with `dependency_overrides` — the first in this
suite, and what planning#167 asks for regardless. It builds a minimal
app carrying the real routers, so the route's declared dependencies are
the thing under test, and additionally asserts (by reading the closure
of each route's `require_role`) that all five target-mutating routes
admit the identical role pair — so a new route added under a different
guard fails.

No rows are written: it PATCHes a random UUID, so ADMIN gets 404 and
VIEWER gets 403, which also proves the 403 is the guard talking and not
a route that stopped working for everyone.

## 2. `GET /api/system/monitoring-status` was unauthenticated

Took only `db`, leaking monitoring cadence (last run / next run) to
anyone who could reach the port. Now requires authentication —
`get_current_user`, not a role gate, since it drives a UI widget.
`/status` stays open deliberately: the first-run bootstrap has to be
readable before any user exists.

## 4. Findings were RESOLVED on a failed verification scan

`_verify_and_resolve` marked a finding RESOLVED after a recheck without
confirming the run reached COMPLETED. A verification scan that crashed
produced exactly the same evidence as one that found nothing — no new
observation — so an operational failure became a reassuring product
state (the planning#160 shape).

`try/except` around the launch does nothing: `scan_executor.launch`
catches its own exceptions and calls `_fail()` internally, so it
**returns `None` on success and `None` on catastrophe**. There is no
exception for the caller to see. The run's own `status` is the only
honest signal, so it is re-read after the launch (`db.expire_all()` was
already there, so the re-read is cheap). The gate is `== COMPLETED`, not
`!= FAILED` — CANCELLED, still-RUNNING and never-started PENDING are all
"we did not look".

**Jason's call on the failure surface** (three options were put to him —
leave it silently, leave it and surface the failure, or a distinct
inconclusive state): **leave the finding untouched and surface the
failure.** Implemented as `detail.last_verification = {outcome, at,
scan_run_id, scan_run_status, error}`, lifted to a top-level
`last_verification` key by `_serialize_finding`. `outcome` is `failed` /
`resolved` / `still_observed`, so a successful re-verify stamps the
finding too. No new `FindingState` value, no migration, nothing
downstream inherits a state it must handle.

Deliberately not on the `verification` / `verified_at` columns: those
belong to the shared-infra verifier and answer a different question (is
this finding attributable to an asset we own). Conflating the ownership
verdict with a recheck scan's outcome would corrupt an axis the claims
layer reads.

`test_verify_failed_scan.py` proves it without mocking the status check
— it makes the executor's `_run` raise and lets `launch`'s own handler
mark the run FAILED, which is the real production path.

## 3. The audit trail — implemented against planning#194's criteria

`audit_logs` shipped in migration 0001 with every column and index it
needs and **no writer**. An empty audit table is worse than none: it
reads as coverage in a design review while no record exists of who added
a target, changed a role or launched a scan.

**One choke point, not per-handler calls.** A per-handler `audit(...)`
call is an opt-in list wearing a different hat — it covers what its
author remembered. `get_current_user` (the one dependency every
authenticated route resolves, and the one `require_role` is built on)
stashes the principal's id on `request.state`; a pure-ASGI
`AuditMiddleware` reads it back off the scope after the response and
writes the row. So "authenticated" and "audited" are the same set **by
construction**.

Pure ASGI rather than `BaseHTTPMiddleware` deliberately: the request
body stream is never touched. The write runs in a threadpool after the
response is sent, on its own session, and a failure is logged at ERROR
and swallowed — an audit trail that can take the API down gets switched
off within a week.

- **Opt-out list**: four entries, each justified in source —
`auth:login`, `auth:refresh`, `auth:setup`, `saml:saml_acs`, all
pre-authentication by definition. Produced by enumeration, which
immediately corrected the hand-written version.
- **Route-enumeration test**: walks every module in `app/api/` and
resolves each mutating route's full dependency tree. It does not assert
"endpoints behind `require_role` produce a row" — that is true by
construction and would be a tautology. It catches the way coverage can
actually be lost: a new mutating endpoint added with *no* guard, which
has no principal to attribute the action to.
- **before/after** via `record_detail()` at the three sites where the
question is asked — `patch_target`, `bulk_set_aggressiveness` (prior
values capped at 50, since the table has no retention sweep),
`users.update`.
- **Secrets**: everything reaching `detail` passes through a recursive
key-name denylist with depth and length caps. Nothing from a request
body is recorded by default.
- **Rejected attempts are recorded**, with the status code in `detail` —
an audit log of successes only cannot answer "who has been trying".
- **Read surface**: `GET /api/audit/` and `/facets`, ADMIN only
(narrower than the pair used to administer — reading the record of what
the admins did is supervisory), plus a third tab on the Activity page,
rendered only for admins so the tab does not exist for a role that would
403 on it.

**On `DELETE /api/logs/`** (planning#162's remaining point, which #194
does not cover): the two are different tables. That endpoint truncates
`system_logs`, a debugging surface an admin is *supposed* to be able to
clear. `audit_logs` is append-only — no delete route (tested), no
retention sweep (tested), one writer (tested by enumerating every file
referencing `AuditLog`) — and clearing the system log is itself audited.
Not claimed: this is API-level; an admin with `psql` can still delete
rows. Tamper-evidence below the API is separate and larger.

## One defect these tests caught

The first audit implementation stashed the `User` object rather than its
id. `get_db`'s session is closed when the response is generated —
*before* the middleware runs — so the object was detached and expired,
and `actor.id` raised `DetachedInstanceError` on every mutating request.
It surfaced only because the audit tests mint real tokens for real user
rows instead of using `dependency_overrides`; overriding
`get_current_user` would have replaced the very code under test and
every assertion would have passed against the bug.

## Verification

- **571 backend tests, green, run twice** (543 before; +28: 7 RBAC, 5
verification, 16 audit).
- **All three fixes mutation-proved.** Restore
`_=Depends(get_current_user)` on `patch_target` → 4 tests fail. Remove

* fix(security): stop leaking passwordHash to the client on /admin/users

/security-review finding (HIGH, data exposure): listUsers() used
Prisma's `include`, which pulled every column off User including
passwordHash. That result was passed as a prop from the server
component AdminUsersPage straight into client components (UsersTable,
EditRolesDialog) typed as the full User model. A Server->Client
Component prop is serialized into the page's RSC payload, so every
user's argon2 hash was shipped to the browser on a page whose UI never
even renders it — turning a lower-severity incident on that page (XSS,
shoulder-surfing, a compromised browser extension) into a full
credential-hash dump.

Fixed by having listUsers() select explicit columns (never
passwordHash) and derive a `hasPassword` boolean server-side for the
one thing the UI actually needed the hash's presence for ("Invite
pending" badge, show/hide "Resend invite"). UsersTable and
EditRolesDialog now take the new SafeUser type instead of Prisma's
full User.
